q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE new military technology introduced during World War I.
parts.b: Explain ONE way in which new military technology contributed to the stalemate on the Western Front, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which governments adapted their economies to support industrial warfare in the period c. 1900–present.

sample_answers.a: The tank — an armored, caterpillar-tracked vehicle armed with guns — was introduced by the British in 1916 to cross trenches and crush barbed wire under machine-gun fire.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, defensive technologies (machine guns, barbed wire, trenches) gave defenders an overwhelming advantage, so new weapons initially strengthened defense more than offense, locking armies into years of attritional stalemate.
sample_answers.c: Governments imposed conscription, directed factories to produce munitions, rationed food and materials, and borrowed heavily — creating the first true 'total war' economies in which the entire society was mobilized for combat.

q1.stimulus:
Historians describe World War I as the first industrial war, in which the technologies of the Second Industrial Revolution were turned to mass killing. The machine gun, rapid-fire artillery, barbed wire, and the trench system gave defenders such overwhelming advantages that offensives became suicidal, producing four years of stalemate. Yet the same industrial system that created the stalemate eventually produced the means to break it: tanks to cross trenches, aircraft to observe and bomb, and poison gas to terrorize. The deeper change was organizational — governments learned to mobilize entire economies for war, conscripting millions of men, directing industry, and borrowing on an unprecedented scale. Warfare was no longer decided mainly by generals' skill but by which society could produce more shells, ships, and soldiers.
—Historian's account of military technology in the period c. 1900–present

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE feature of the tank described in the account.
parts.b: Describe ONE way in which tanks addressed the problems of trench warfare.
parts.c: Explain ONE limitation of early tanks as suggested by the account.

sample_answers.a: The account describes an armored vehicle moving on caterpillar tracks, protected against rifle and machine-gun fire, and armed with guns to attack enemy positions.
sample_answers.b: Tanks could crush barbed wire, cross trenches on their tracks, and advance against machine-gun fire that would slaughter infantry — directly overcoming the three main obstacles of the Western Front.
sample_answers.c: The account suggests the tanks were slow, mechanically unreliable, and few in number; they broke down frequently and could not exploit breakthroughs, limiting their impact in 1916.

q2.stimulus:
At dawn the strange new engines moved forward toward the German lines. They advanced slowly on their endless caterpillar tracks, crushing the barbed wire beneath their weight as though it were straw. Rifle and machine-gun bullets rattled harmlessly against their armored sides. The German soldiers, who had never seen such machines, fled in terror from their trenches. Yet for all their promise, the monsters were few and frail: several broke down before reaching the enemy, and those that survived could barely crawl faster than a walking man.
—Adapted from a British officer's account of the first tank attack, Battle of Flers-Courcelette, 15 September 1916

q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE feature of the tank visible in the photograph.
parts.b: Explain ONE reason why tanks were developed during World War I.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which armored warfare changed military tactics in the twentieth century after World War I.

sample_answers.a: The photograph shows a rhomboid-shaped armored vehicle with caterpillar tracks designed to cross trenches, carrying guns in side sponsons — the distinctive silhouette of the British Mark I tank.
sample_answers.b: Tanks were developed to break the trench stalemate: only an armored vehicle could cross no-man's-land, crush wire, and survive machine-gun fire to restore mobility to the battlefield.
sample_answers.c: Armored vehicles enabled the fast-moving Blitzkrieg tactics of World War II, in which concentrated tank formations punched through defenses and exploited into the enemy rear — making the static trench warfare of 1914–18 obsolete.

q3.stimulus: The photograph shows a British Mark I tank advancing at Flers-Courcelette on 15 September 1916, during the Battle of the Somme — the first use of tanks in warfare. The rhomboid-shaped vehicle, moving on caterpillar tracks and armed with guns mounted in side sponsons, was designed to cross trenches and crush barbed wire. Though only a handful were available and many broke down, their debut marked the beginning of armored warfare.
